note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Colossians 3:11 ends, “but Christ is all, and in all.” Now they will say, see, Christ is in all. Then they go to Acts 10: “Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.”

Read the whole thing: “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: (he is Lord of all:)” Lord of all what? Lord of all Israel, scattered in every nation.

And Paul clears it up himself in the very next verse of Colossians: “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved.” Isaiah 45:4 says “Israel mine elect”; Leviticus 20:26 says the Lord has “severed you from other people”; Baruch calls Israel “his beloved.” He is speaking in a language we can understand, not for the heathen. They know good and well this Bible does not belong to them, but in slavery they played on our ignorance. Now the God of Israel has poured His spirit on His people in these last days, and we know what the Bible is talking about.

precepts.why:
Cornelius is called “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.” How do you become a devout man? People go, yeah, he was another nation, but he was devout. No, no, no.

Look at how the scripture uses the word: “And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. You see? A devout man according to the law. The other nations did not have the law.

So how was Cornelius a devout man according to the law? How did he fear God? How did he know how to pray to God? He had to know the law. He even kept the hours of prayer: the angel came to him “about the ninth hour of the day”, and he told Peter, “at the ninth hour I prayed in my house”.

So yes, Cornelius is an Israelite, northern kingdom. His devotion was devotion to the law of God, which was given to Israel and to no other nation.

And Acts shows believers coming out of that very place: “There went with us also certain of the disciples of Cesarea, and brought with them one Mnason of Cyprus, an old disciple, with whom we should lodge.” You had some disciples that came from Caesarea as well, the same place Cornelius is from.

Peter lived in Joppa, the seaport there, and he sailed up north to visit Cornelius. Christ was raised further up, in Galilee, so he was raised around them in that area. And the place called Scythopolis means city of the Scythians, and the Scythians are northern kingdom also: that is who Paul wrote to in Colossians 3:11.

So Caesarea was a place of disciples in the land of Manasseh, and Cornelius and his kinsmen were northern kingdom Israelites living in their own land, not a Roman people God took in instead of Israel.

That is why the dream was never about eating unclean animals. Verse 28 is where Peter breaks the dream down: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” Any man. It is not talking about roaches or ants or eating unclean pig. The dream was about man.

What man? The Israelites being cleansed, the northern kingdom being cleansed. The vessel full of fourfooted beasts and creeping things is Israel scattered among the Gentiles, and God was showing Peter it was time to bring them back in.

Then: “but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.” God says he is going to cleanse us, the twelve tribes.

So what God hath cleansed is Israel, the northern kingdom brought back to Judah. That is why Peter could go into Cornelius’ house. James in Acts 15 was quoting the prophet Amos. This is what James and Peter were quoting: “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof”. He is going to bring back the southern kingdom with the northern kingdom.

“And I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old”: as in the days of old, when the twelve tribes were one.

“That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name”. The heathen called by his name are those that call themselves Jewish and those that call themselves Christian. Christian is a Greek word that means anointed ones. They are not the anointed ones. We are.

So Cornelius and his house being accepted was the word of Amos coming to pass: the breach between the kingdoms being closed up, the tabernacle of David raised, and Israel set to possess the remnant of Edom, “saith the Lord that doeth this.”

Ephraim and the tribes of Israel his fellows are the northern kingdom; the stick of Judah is the southern kingdom. God puts them together and makes them one stick in his hand.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Cornelius is called “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house”. What does it mean to be devout? Acts 22 shows it: “And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there”. To be devout is to be devout according to the law, and to have a good report for it.

So when Acts 10 says Cornelius was a devout man, it is saying he was a law-abiding man. He kept the laws of God. He feared God with all his house, gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.

His own messengers tell Peter the same thing later in the chapter: “Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews”. The same good report Ananias had among the Jews, Cornelius had too.

That is why Peter came to understand that the vision was about man, not food, and that he should not call any man common or unclean. Cornelius was a just man and a devout man, a keeper of the law. “God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.”

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
The angel tells Cornelius, “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.” How do prayers come up before God? Tobit shows it. The angel Raphael says, “I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, which present the prayers of the saints, and which go in and out before the glory of the Holy One.”

These are the angels that bring your prayers before the Most High God. Cornelius saw “an angel of God coming in to him” about the ninth hour, and that angel came because his prayers had gone up and been presented before the Holy One.

So when Acts 10 says his prayers and alms came up “for a memorial before God”, it is speaking of this very thing: the holy angels going in and out before the glory of God, presenting the prayers of those who fear him.

And the answer came back down by the same way. The angel told Cornelius to send men to Joppa and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter, who would tell him what he ought to do.

precepts.text: Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness. When you pray to God, if you combine it with alms and fasting, the prayers are heard before the Most High. That is exactly what we read of Cornelius in Acts 10:2 and 10:4.
precepts.point: A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. His prayers and his alms came up for a memorial before God, and the angel told him to send men to Joppa and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
In the same chapter where Raphael says he presents the prayers of the saints, he says what makes those prayers go up: “Prayer is good with fasting and alms and righteousness.” Prayer joined with fasting and alms and being righteous is what makes your prayers go before the Lord.

In other words, when you pray to God and combine it with alms and fasting, the prayers are heard before the Most High. That is exactly what we read of Cornelius in Acts 10:2: “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.”

And it is exactly what the angel told him in Acts 10:4: “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.” Not his prayers alone, but his prayers and his alms together, from a devout man who kept the law.

So Cornelius is the example of what Tobit teaches. His righteousness, his alms and his praying alway went up before God, and God answered by sending him to Peter.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Peter fell into a trance and saw a vessel full of “fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air”, and a voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” Peter answered, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” But the vision was not really talking about food. That is why it says “Peter doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen should mean”.

When visions come from God, they are an allegory, referring to something else many times. The Lord proves it himself: “I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets.” A similitude shows you one thing, but it is really something else he is trying to explain.

That is what Peter was pondering. Is the Lord telling me to eat unlawful animals? No, Lord, I have never eaten anything unlawful. The beasts in the sheet were a similitude, and Peter did not yet know what they stood for.

He found out when he came to Cornelius. He said, “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” The vision was not about unclean animals; it was about man. Cornelius was a just man and a devout man, and the vision was showing Peter that God is no respecter of persons, northern kingdom or southern kingdom: “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” Israel, the ones called not God’s people, would one day be joined back in.

precepts.why:
Peter says, “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” Every nation: Acts 2 shows who was in every nation. “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.”

They had come together for the feast of Pentecost: “And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place.” These were devout Jews, devout like Cornelius, gathered out of every nation where they had been scattered. So “every nation” in Peter’s words is not every race of people; it is the Israelites living in every nation under heaven.

And God received them. “Suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind”, “cloven tongues like as of fire” sat upon each of them, “And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.”

That is what Peter came to understand at Cornelius’ house. God is no respecter of persons, northern kingdom or southern kingdom. Those that keep the commandments have a place of repentance, and Israel, the ones that were called not God’s people, would one day be joined back in.

The vessel in Peter's vision was “knit at the four corners.” The four corners are in the prophets too: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

So what is in that sheet, gathered at the four corners? It was Israel, scattered through the four corners of the earth, living as beasts. The outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah are the ones God assembles from those four corners.

He sets up an ensign “for the nations” because Israel would be scattered among all the nations and live as Gentiles. The picture of a sheet knit at four corners is the picture of God drawing his scattered people together from every end of the earth, and that is the vision Peter had to explain to those of the circumcision.

This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear it, they think it is everybody. No: God said Israel was the vessel.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
In the vessel were “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.” Peter had to explain to the circumcision, who contended with him, that the fourfooted beasts, the wild beasts, the creeping things and the fowls of the air refer to man. So there had to be scripture to prove it.

Ezra prays: “Let it not be thy will to destroy them which have lived like beasts; but to look upon them that have clearly taught thy law.” There are men who have lived like beasts, and Ezra pleads with God not to destroy them. So we know the beast refers to man.

The vision was not about animals; it was about men. Israel, scattered and living like beasts without the law, is what was let down in that sheet, and Ezra's prayer is that God would spare them and look upon those who teach his law.

precepts.text: So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.
precepts.point: Now the scriptures substantiate the vision Peter had. The vessel knit at the four corners is Israel, and the beasts within it are men. This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear it, they think it is everybody. No: God said Israel was the vessel.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Another witness that the beasts in Peter's sheet are men: the psalmist says of himself, “So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.”

A man, foolish and ignorant before God, is called a beast. So when Peter explained the vision to those of the circumcision who contended with him, he could say: remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts before God.

That is the whole key to Acts 10. The fourfooted beasts in the vessel are not pork and shellfish made clean. They are the people of Israel who were foolish and ignorant, living as beasts before the Lord, whom God was now going to cleanse and gather back together.

precepts.text: Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net. When Peter explained the fourfooted beasts and wild beasts, he would have to refer to these scriptures: remember, it is written that we lived as beasts, that we were as a wild bull.
precepts.point: Now the scriptures substantiate the vision Peter had. The vessel knit at the four corners is Israel, and the beasts within it are men. This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear it, they think it is everybody. No: God said Israel was the vessel.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
The vessel also held “wild beasts.” Isaiah names them: “Thy sons have fainted, they lie at the head of all the streets, as a wild bull in a net: they are full of the fury of the Lord, the rebuke of thy God.”

The sons of Israel, fainted and lying at the head of every street, are compared to a wild bull caught in a net, full of the fury of the Lord. The wild beast is a man of Israel under God's rebuke.

When Peter explained the fourfooted beasts and wild beasts, he would have to refer to scriptures like these. Remember, it is written in 2 Esdras that we lived as beasts. Remember, it is written in Psalms that we were as beasts. Remember, Isaiah the prophet said we would be as a wild bull. The vision was about men, and the scriptures prove it.

precepts.text: And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them. When we were without God, with no ruler, we were like creeping things; without the laws of God we were like beasts.
precepts.point: Now the scriptures substantiate the vision Peter had. The vessel knit at the four corners is Israel, and the beasts within it are men. This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear it, they think it is everybody. No: God said Israel was the vessel.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
The vessel also held “creeping things.” Who are the creeping things? The vision was not about animals; it was about man, so there has to be a scripture showing that the creeping thing refers to man. Habakkuk says to God: “And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?”

Men made as creeping things that have no ruler over them. When we were without God, with no ruler, we were like creeping things, like insects or bugs. Without the laws of God, we were like beasts, like animals.

So every creature in Peter's sheet is a description of Israel scattered without God and without his law. The creeping things are men with no ruler over them, and God was about to bring them back under his rule.

precepts.text: Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven. The fowls of the air also refer to man. Imagine those of the circumcision hearing Peter refer to Hosea: remember, he called us fowls. That is why the scripture says prove all things: everything must be proven as it is written, that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and overcome when thou art judged.
precepts.point: Now the scriptures substantiate the vision Peter had. The vessel knit at the four corners is Israel, and the beasts within it are men. This is why the nations cannot handle us right now: when we speak, we can use the Bible to explain itself. When they hear it, they think it is everybody. No: God said Israel was the vessel.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
The last creatures in the vessel are the “fowls of the air.” There had to be scripture to show that the fowls of the air also refer to man. Hosea says: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria. When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard.”

Ephraim, the northern kingdom, is the silly dove, brought down as the fowls of the heaven. So the fowls in Peter's vision are Israelites too.

Now imagine those of the circumcision hearing Peter speak: listen, over here in Hosea, remember, God called us fowls. God was showing him it was time to gather the twelve tribes, north and south, back together.

That is why the scripture says prove all things. Everything must be proven as it is written, that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and overcome when thou art judged. Peter did not just tell a vision; he could prove every creature in it from the prophets.

precepts.text: Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west unto the east by the word of the Holy One. By this word is what is going to gather the children of Israel back together. He is telling Peter: it is time; awake; rise; now it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel.
precepts.point: Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. Kill: kill the old man, mortify yourself, discipline yourself. Eat: devour wisdom, learn the scripture. And then go out and teach. But in that time there was no New Testament: Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
We know now the vision is referring to man. So what is the “Rise” talking about? What was the whole purpose of the vision? To gather the northern and southern kingdoms back together, to gather us back from where we were scattered, east to west, north and south.

Baruch uses the same word: “Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high, and look about toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west unto the east by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of God.” The children are coming from the west unto the east, and they rejoice when they remember God.

They are gathered “by the word of the Holy One.” That word is what is going to gather the children of Israel back together. This is it right here.

So when the voice says “Rise, Peter”, he is telling Peter: it is time. Awake. Rise. Now it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. The arising comes first; then comes the kill and the eat, because before we gather the twelve tribes we first have to be made ready to teach them.

precepts.text: A brother said kill means kill the old man, as in Romans 6; but Peter would have needed the Old Testament: thou shalt mortify it as thy creature, and quicken it as thy work. Mortify, deaden, kill the old man, and be quickened.
precepts.point: Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. Kill: kill the old man, mortify yourself, discipline yourself. Eat: devour wisdom, learn the scripture. And then go out and teach. But in that time there was no New Testament: Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
“Rise, Peter; kill”. What does kill mean? A brother answered: kill the old man, the old mindset, as it is written in Romans 6. That is right. But in that time there was no New Testament. Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

Ezra gives it: “Thou broughtest it up with thy righteousness, and nurturedst it in thy law, and reformedst it with thy judgment. And thou shalt mortify it as thy creature, and quicken it as thy work.” That is what you do. You have to mortify, deaden, kill the old man, and be quickened as God’s work.

That is the “kill” in Peter’s vision. Rise, Peter, and kill the old man. Mortify yourself. Discipline yourself. The man God brings up in his righteousness, nurtures in his law and reforms with his judgment is the man who has put the old man to death.

Only after the old man is killed can you eat, learn the scripture, and then go out and teach. That is the order God gave Peter before sending him to gather the northern kingdom.

precepts.text: Swallow down understanding, O my soul, and devour wisdom: that is the eating; you have to learn. For thou hast agreed to give ear, and art willing to prophesy: after you learn, you go out and prophesy. Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes. Kill the old man; mortify yourself. Eat; devour wisdom. Then go out and prophesy.
precepts.point: Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. Kill: kill the old man, mortify yourself, discipline yourself. Eat: devour wisdom, learn the scripture. And then go out and teach. But in that time there was no New Testament: Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
After “kill” comes “eat”. What does eat mean? Learn the scripture. Ezra says it plainly: “Swallow then down, O my soul, understanding, and devour wisdom.” That is the eating. You have to go out and learn.

And after you learn, what do you do? “For thou hast agreed to give ear, and art willing to prophesy: for thou hast no longer space than only to live.” You gave ear, you devoured wisdom, and now you are willing to prophesy. After you learn, you go out and prophesy.

So the whole vision is laid out. Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel back together. Kill, Peter: kill the old man, mortify yourself. Eat, Peter: devour wisdom. Then go out and prophesy.

This is the Old Testament way Peter would have explained it to those of the circumcision: the eating in the vision was never about unclean beasts, but about swallowing down understanding so he could teach the scattered of Israel.

precepts.text: The same pattern: take the little book and eat it up; and thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings. You have to eat, learn, and then you must go out and prophesy.
precepts.point: Rise, Peter: it is time to gather the twelve tribes of Israel. Kill: kill the old man, mortify yourself, discipline yourself. Eat: devour wisdom, learn the scripture. And then go out and teach. But in that time there was no New Testament: Peter would have to explain it to those of the circumcision using the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Revelation says the same thing. John went to the angel and said, “Give me the little book. And he said unto me, Take it, and eat it up; and it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey.” John “took the little book out of the angel’s hand, and ate it up”, and it was sweet as honey in his mouth, and as soon as he had eaten it his belly was bitter.

Then comes the reason for the eating: “Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings.” The book is eaten so that it can be prophesied.

That is the same pattern as “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” You have to eat, you have to learn, and then you must go out and prophesy. John ate the book and was sent before many peoples and nations; Peter was told to eat and was sent to the house of Cornelius.

So eating in the vision means taking in the word. Rise, kill the old man, eat the word, and go out and prophesy to the scattered tribes.

precepts.text: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men. Peter understood that common was tied to evil.
precepts.point: And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. The subject matter of the cleansing is man; and to explain that cleansing, Peter would have to use the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Peter answered the vision, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” To understand what he meant by common, go to Solomon: “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men”.

Common is tied to evil. Peter understood that. So when he said he had never eaten anything common, he was not only talking about meat. In other words: I have never done sin, I have never dealt with sin, I have never dealt with people that were evil.

That is why the vision had to be explained to him. The sheet let down from heaven was not about food; it was about men, and Peter was being told to go among people he had counted as common.

precepts.text: They will give thereof to the common harlots: common used again for evil. So when Peter said, I have never eaten anything common or unclean, he was saying, I have never dealt with sinners.
precepts.point: And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. The subject matter of the cleansing is man; and to explain that cleansing, Peter would have to use the Old Testament.

note.label: Acts 10 Reloaded: Call No Man Common

precepts.why:
Baruch shows the word common used again for evil. Speaking of the idolaters and their gods, “they will give thereof to the common harlots, and deck them as men with garments, being gods of silver, and gods of gold, and wood.” The common harlots: the word goes with whoredom and idolatry.

So when Peter said, “I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean”, he was saying, I have never dealt with sinners. I have never sat down with them.

But then the voice spake unto him again the second time, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” What had God cleansed? The subject matter is man. And to explain that cleansing to those of the circumcision, Peter would have to go to the Old Testament: to Ezekiel 37, where God would save them out of their dwelling places and cleanse them, take the children of Israel from among the heathen and make two kingdoms one; and to Hosea 1, where in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, it would be said, Ye are the sons of the living God.

The time had come to gather the northern kingdom back together. And that is happening now: God's people are being gathered in South America, in Africa and here in the States.

precepts.text: I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel, and they shall be no more two nations. The kingdom of Judah was called a nation and the kingdom of Israel was called a nation: two nations, one people.
precepts.point: Peter saw the vision of the sheet with all manner of beasts and heard, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat. Verse 28 is the breakdown: ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. The other nation here is the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom.

note.label: Recovering the Remnant: Worldwide Blitz

precepts.why:
Peter says, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. That phrase “another nation” might throw you off, because Christians use it to say Peter was going to other races. Ezekiel shows what that other nation is: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”.

The kingdom of Judah was called a nation, and the kingdom of Israel, Ephraim and the rest, was called a nation. Two nations, two separate kingdoms, but one people. So when Peter the Jew, of Judah, speaks of coming unto one of another nation, that other nation is the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. That is what the vision of the sheet was about: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean”, speaking of Cornelius and his family.

Then Peter says God “is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” A Christian will stop you right there, but read the next verse: “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”. That tells you who Cornelius and his kinfolk were: the children of Israel, scattered in every nation.

Acts 15 looks back on this and quotes the prophets: “After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down”. The regathering of the twelve tribes, the two kingdoms coming back together, is what Acts 10 is about. God is bringing the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom back into one nation, just as Ezekiel said.

precepts.text: How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power. Christ is the most Holy anointed at the end of Daniel 9:24.
precepts.point: He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the midst of the week cause the sacrifice and oblation to cease, with the overspreading of abominations in the temple that Christ warned of. All seventy weeks are fulfilled. Amalek tells Christians the last week is future and belongs to a rebuilt temple, counting on blacks and Latinos not understanding the scriptures.

note.label: Prophesy From Pain to Peace

precepts.why:
Seventy weeks are determined “to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.” To make an end of sins is Christ coming to die, and the reconciliation for iniquity is all through Christ.

And who is the most Holy that is anointed? “How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.” Christ is the anointed one.

So the bottom of Daniel 9:24, “to anoint the most Holy”, is Christ, anointed as the most Holy. That is why the seventy weeks run unto “the Messiah the Prince”: the whole prophecy is counted to him and fulfilled in him.

precepts.text: Manasseh's coast reached to the sea and included the inhabitants of Dor and her towns.
precepts.point: He lived at Caesarea Maritima, the old Strato's Tower below Dor, in the land of West Manasseh. He was devout, gave alms to the people and prayed always, like Tobit.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Where is Cornelius from? Some people say Italy. He is from Cesarea. There are three Caesareas: one in Africa, which is not written of, Caesarea Philippi, and Caesarea Maritima. Cornelius is from Caesarea Maritima, the place the maps call Strato's Tower, right under Dor, in Samaria, the same country where Christ spoke to the woman at the well. When Rome colonized our land they named it for Caesar, and Maritima because it is a port on the water. And the maps mark that land West Manasseh.

Somebody will say that's just a map, it ain't in the Bible. So here it is in the Bible, for the doubters: “And the coast of Manasseh was from Asher to Michmethah, that lieth before Shechem; and the border went along on the right hand unto the inhabitants of En–tappuah.”

Read on. “Now Manasseh had the land of Tappuah: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim”. The coast went down to the river Kanah: “the coast of Manasseh also was on the north side of the river, and the outgoings of it were at the sea”. “Southward it was Ephraim’s, and northward it was Manasseh’s, and the sea is his border”: the Mediterranean Sea. Peter dwelt in Joppa and went some thirty to forty miles up the coast to Caesarea Maritima, just before Dor.

Then verse 11: “And Manasseh had in Issachar and in Asher Beth–shean and her towns, and Ibleam and her towns, and the inhabitants of Dor and her towns”. Under Dor was Caesarea Maritima; that was all Dor before. Endor, Taanach and Megiddo were Manasseh's too. “Yet the children of Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants of those cities; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.” There were too many of them to conquer them all.

So that is Manasseh's land. It is called West Manasseh because Manasseh also dwelt on the other side of Jordan, East Manasseh. This was once Manasseh's allotment right under Ephraim, the sons of Joseph. Asher shared that port, but the land was Manasseh's.

Cornelius was not Italian. He was of the Italian band, a unit of the Roman army. There were Israelites in Rome's military, just as there are Israelites in America's military today. But negroes love master so much they see the word Italian and get excited: yes, he's white, I knew it. No, he was of the Italian band, from Caesarea, West Manasseh, one of the northern kingdom. A centurion was over a hundred men. He was “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway”, the exact same thing Tobit said he did.

precepts.text: Israel is swallowed up among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.
precepts.point: What God hath cleansed, call not thou common. As at Hezekiah's Passover, God pardoned and cleansed northern Israelites who sought him, and the vision has nothing to do with eating pork.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Peter saw “a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners”. A vessel knit at the four corners. Remember the Lord told Jacob his children would be scattered abroad to the north, east, south and west. Hosea says what that vessel is: “Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.”

A vessel wherein is no pleasure means unclean, no good, unable to be used. Vessels were used in the temple for service, but a vessel in which there is no pleasure cannot be used for temple service; it is deemed unclean. That is Israel scattered among the nations, counted unclean.

So the vessel full of “all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air” is Israel scattered to the four corners and swallowed up among the Gentiles. Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” But “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” It is not talking about no damn animals; it isn't about pork.

At Hezekiah's Passover many of Ephraim and Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun “had not cleansed themselves”, yet Hezekiah prayed, “The good Lord pardon every one That prepareth his heart to seek God”, and “the Lord hearkened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.” Cornelius, of West Manasseh, was a devout man who prepared his heart to seek God. God cleansed that vessel of no pleasure, and Peter learned he “should not call any man common or unclean.”

precepts.text: He shall assemble the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
precepts.point: What God hath cleansed, call not thou common. As at Hezekiah's Passover, God pardoned and cleansed northern Israelites who sought him, and the vision has nothing to do with eating pork.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
The sheet Peter saw was “knit at the four corners”, and Isaiah shows why: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.”

The nations here are Israel. He will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah, as Hosea said, from the four corners of the earth. A vessel knit at the four corners: that is Israel scattered to every corner, and the Lord gathering them.

That is what the vision meant. Peter doubted in himself what it should mean, thinking what Christians think, that he was told to eat unclean food. But he saw it three times, and three men came from Cornelius. Then he understood: “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.” The vision was about a man, Cornelius, one of the outcasts of Israel from the northern kingdom whom Judah called common and unclean.

What God hath cleansed, call not thou common: the Lord is gathering both houses, the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah, and making them clean, one nation again, as Ezekiel said, “neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”.

precepts.text: They shall be no more two nations, neither divided into two kingdoms any more.
precepts.point: The other nation is the northern kingdom, the company of nations. God promised to make the two one nation and cleanse them.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Peter said, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation”. Sound familiar? It is the same thing the woman at the well said to Christ: the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. “but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean”. Any man, not food, not animals. The vision was about a man, Cornelius.

Who is one of another nation? In Genesis 35 Jacob was told a nation and a company of nations would come of him. Ezekiel shows the two becoming one: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”. Judah and Ephraim, both the houses, gathered together under one king.

“Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions: but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.” He will cleanse both kingdoms and make them clean.

So Cornelius was of another nation, another kingdom: the northern kingdom. Judah called the northern kingdom common and unclean, not my people, strangers. But what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. God promised to cleanse them and make the two one nation, and that is why Peter could go into Cornelius's house.

precepts.text: There were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.
precepts.point: The word was sent unto the children of Israel, and Peter told Cornelius, that word ye know. Remission of sins through Christ is given to his people.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Peter said, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.” In every nation, because Israel is in every nation. Luke shows it at Pentecost: “And there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.”

Israel is scattered everywhere, to all four corners: that is the vessel knit at the four corners in Peter's vision. So “in every nation he that feareth him” is not every people on earth; it is the Israelites scattered in every nation who fear God and work righteousness, like Cornelius, a devout man who feared God with all his house and gave much alms.

And read the next verse; they always skip it. “The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ”. The word was sent to the children of Israel. Those accepted in every nation are the children of Israel in every nation.

precepts.text: Deliverance is in Mount Zion and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.
precepts.point: The word was sent unto the children of Israel, and Peter told Cornelius, that word ye know. Remission of sins through Christ is given to his people.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
Peter told Cornelius, “To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.” Isn't that what Cornelius was receiving? Joel is one of the prophets giving that witness: “And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered”.

That word whosoever again. But where is the deliverance? Not in all the heathen nations: “for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the Lord hath said, and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”

The whosoever is the remnant whom the Lord shall call. Peter said to Cornelius, “That word, I say, ye know”: the Samaritans and the northern kingdom knew it, as Isaiah said Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria shall know, and as the woman at the well said, I know that Messias cometh. Cornelius was devout; he knew the law and that he would be called eventually. He was of that remnant.

precepts.text: He hath visited and redeemed his people, to give knowledge of salvation unto his people.
precepts.point: The word was sent unto the children of Israel, and Peter told Cornelius, that word ye know. Remission of sins through Christ is given to his people.

note.label: The Dividing Hatred: Cornelius the Centurion

precepts.why:
“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people”. The Lord God of Israel visited and redeemed his people, not every people.

Read on to verse 77: “To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins”. To whom? Unto his people. Remission of whose sins? Their sins.

So the word Peter brought to Cornelius was for the remission of their sins, and that includes Cornelius too. “in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him” because Cornelius was one of his people, an Israelite of the northern kingdom in West Manasseh, whom the Lord God of Israel came to visit and redeem. Acts 15 says it: “God at the first did visit the Gentiles, to take out of them a people for his name.” That visit, beginning with Cornelius, is the building again of the tabernacle of David, all twelve tribes reunited.

precepts.text: It was counted unlawful for a man that is a Jew to keep company with one of another nation; the split between the kingdoms ran that deep.
precepts.point: Joash took Amaziah, came to Jerusalem, and broke down the wall of Jerusalem four hundred cubits. He took all the gold and silver and the vessels found in the house of the Most High, and the treasures of the king's house, and hostages, and returned to Samaria. The two kingdoms had real animosity, calling each other another nation, brother stealing the vessels out of his own brother's temple.

note.label: 2 Chronicles 25: Amaziah Serves the Most High With a Divided Heart

precepts.why:
Peter said, “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation.” It was counted unlawful for a man that is a Jew to keep company with one of another nation, and the split between the kingdoms ran that deep.

The two kingdoms had real animosity, calling each other another nation. Amaziah, lifted up after he had “smitten the Edomites”, sent to Joash king of Israel, “Come, let us see one another in the face.” Joash answered with the parable of “The thistle that was in Lebanon” and “the cedar that was in Lebanon”, and told him, “thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to thine hurt”.

“But Amaziah would not hear; for it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom.” “Judah was put to the worse before Israel, and they fled every man to his tent.” Joash “brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits”, and took “all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God”, the treasures of the king’s house and the hostages, and returned to Samaria. Brother stealing the vessels out of his own brother’s temple.

note.label: Psalm 132: The Oath to David and the Throne Forever

“When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.” Peter, in Acts, is one of those disciples telling it after it came to pass.

Correcting a misheard reference to Luke 3, the centurions of scripture were often Israelite servants in the army.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“There was a certain man in Cesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band.” When our people read “Italian band” they automatically picture a Caucasian. But Caesarea Maritima sat on a seacoast in the land of Israel, and Cornelius was an Israelite officer in the Roman army, not a man of another nation.

It was common for Israelites to live in Italy and Rome. Paul “found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:)”. A Jew born in Pontus, living in Italy, and there were enough Jews in Rome for Claudius to command them all to depart.

Jews of the diaspora were fully enmeshed in Roman culture. They took Greek and Latin names and built careers in the Roman military, so a black man, an Israelite, serving under the Italian band is nothing strange. It is the same as so-called black people and Latinos serving in the American military today, from the Buffalo Soldiers to a general like Colin Powell.

precepts.text: Ananias is called "a devout man according to the law," so devout is always measured by keeping the law.
precepts.point: Scholars themselves suppose from this language that Cornelius was a Jew or a proselyte instructed in the Jewish religion, because the pagan Romans worshipped the sun, the moon, and gods like Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Hermes, not the commandments.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
Cornelius was “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway.” To be devout is to be devout according to the law, a man who keeps the commandments.

Scripture measures it that way: “one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt there.” Devout is always measured by keeping the law. So when Cornelius is called devout, he is being called a keeper of the commandments.

precepts.text: He sheweth his word, statutes, and judgments unto Jacob and Israel, and dealt so with no other nation.

The law, the statutes and the judgments were shown to Jacob and to Israel only, never to any other nation. So a man keeping the commandments and called devout is being marked as an Israelite. Israel followed the nations into idolatry; the nations never turned around and started keeping the law of the Most High.

Israel by name kept the precepts; the heathen did not. So a commandment-keeper is Israel. Cornelius, devout, fearing God with all his house, giving alms and praying always, is keeping the precepts, and that marks him as an Israelite and not one of the heathen.

precepts.text: The fear of the Most High is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding belongs to all they that do his commandments.
precepts.point: Scholars themselves suppose from this language that Cornelius was a Jew or a proselyte instructed in the Jewish religion, because the pagan Romans worshipped the sun, the moon, and gods like Mars, Venus, Jupiter, and Hermes, not the commandments.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments.”

To fear the Most High is to keep his commandments. So when Cornelius is called “one that feared God with all his house”, he is a man that does the commandments, and with his whole house. That is the law, which was given to Israel only.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.”

precepts.text: Esau was rejected and found no place of repentance though he sought it with tears, so salvation opening to Cornelius proves he was not of Esau's Rome.
precepts.point: Scholars also record that Esau is the forefather of the Roman Empire, so if Cornelius were truly a Roman he would be an Edomite, and the Most High rejected Esau. This is the proof that Cornelius could not be a Roman by nation, because a Roman would have no place of repentance.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.”

Esau was rejected and found no place of repentance, though he sought it with tears. A Roman, being of Esau, would have no place of repentance. So salvation opening to Cornelius is the proof that he was not of Esau's Rome. He could not be a Roman by nation.

precepts.point: Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed, and the Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

“When the Lord shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory. He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.” And he looks down from heaven “To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death.”

Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed. The Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

precepts.point: Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed, and the Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel’s hand.”

The prayers that ascend before the Most High are the prayers of the saints, and the saints are Israel. So when Cornelius' prayers “are come up for a memorial before God”, they are rising the way the prayers of the saints rise.

precepts.text: He exalts the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints, even the children of Israel.
precepts.point: Israel were the prisoners of Rome, the oppressed, and the Most High hears the prayer of the oppressed, not the prayer of the oppressor. Salvation coming up as a memorial belongs to Zion and to Jerusalem, not to the captor.

“He also exalteth the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints; even of the children of Israel, a people near unto him.”

Scripture says plainly who the saints are: “even of the children of Israel.” The prayers that come up before him are the prayers of his saints, the people near unto him. Cornelius' prayers came up for a memorial before God because he was of that people.

precepts.point: The beasts, creeping things, and fowls are men, because scripture testifies that men in their estate are as beasts, so the whole allegory is about the state of the northern kingdom, not about food.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

Peter saw “a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth.” Christians use this vision to justify eating unclean food, but it is symbolic, and it points back to the northern kingdom.

The vessel is Israel: “Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.” Israel, swallowed up among the nations, is that vessel let down to Peter.

precepts.text: Israel did not destroy the nations but mingled among the heathen, learned their works, and served their idols.
precepts.point: The beasts, creeping things, and fowls are men, because scripture testifies that men in their estate are as beasts, so the whole allegory is about the state of the northern kingdom, not about food.

That is the state of the northern kingdom. Israel did not destroy the nations but mingled among the heathen, learned their works and served their idols. That is why the vessel in Peter's vision is full of every kind of beast: it shows Israel after mingling among the nations, not a lesson about food.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek.” The Gentiles who seek him are the remnant of his people: “the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.”

“And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” That is the sheet knit at the four corners. It is the Israelite diaspora, the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah gathered from the four corners of the earth, which is why the Most High used a sheet from four corners.

“The envy also of Ephraim shall depart”, “Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.” The northern kingdom and the southern kingdom are gathered together, and that is what was let down to Peter.

precepts.text: God manifests that the sons of men, in their estate, might see that they themselves are beasts, so the beasts in the sheet are men.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“I said in mine heart concerning the estate of the sons of men, that God might manifest them, and that they might see that they themselves are beasts.”

The beasts, creeping things and fowls in the sheet are men. Scripture testifies that men in their estate are as beasts. So the whole allegory is about the state of the northern kingdom, mingled among the nations, and not about food.

Nothing in the vision changed the nature of any animal.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
A voice said, “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat.” Peter answered, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.” Peter refuses because he knows the dietary law: “This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.”

There is a beast that may be eaten and a beast that may not. The Most High did not change the duty of a pig, a hawk or a vulture. The unclean animals are the scavengers, the garbage disposal of the earth, made to filter the filth, while the clean animals have a filtration system so their meat is safe. Nothing in the vision changed the nature of any animal.

precepts.text: He will save them out of all their dwellings where they sinned and cleanse them, so they shall be his people; this is the man that is cleansed.
precepts.point: The northern kingdom was planted a holy and righteous seed, so it can be cleansed again, unlike the unclean animals that were made unclean from the beginning. The Most High promised to save Israel out of all their dwelling places where they had sinned and to cleanse them.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

He promised it: “Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions: but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God.” That is the man that is cleansed: Israel, saved out of all the places where they sinned.

precepts.text: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one, which speaks of the animals, while Israel as a planted holy seed can be cleansed.
precepts.point: The northern kingdom was planted a holy and righteous seed, so it can be cleansed again, unlike the unclean animals that were made unclean from the beginning. The Most High promised to save Israel out of all their dwelling places where they had sinned and to cleanse them.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.”

That speaks of the animals. The unclean animals were made unclean from the beginning, and no prayer makes them clean. But the northern kingdom was planted a holy and righteous seed, so it can be cleansed again. That is why the Most High can say, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common”: he is speaking of Israel, not of swine.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

“Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” To be just is to keep the law that is holy, just and good. A just man is one who keeps the law.

Even the southern kingdom, which had no dealings with the north, understood that this particular man of the northern tribes kept the commandments and had a good reputation, like Tobit before him. So they vouched for him by his pattern of good works and alms.

precepts.text: Israel says, "What portion have we in David?" and departs to their tents, and only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David.
precepts.point: The division began when Rehoboam refused the people and Jeroboam led the ten tribes away, so the southern kingdom (Judah, Benjamin, Levi) and the northern kingdom went their separate ways, and the Levites and a remnant that set their hearts to seek the Most High left the north and came to Judah. note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

The division began when Rehoboam refused the people: “the king hearkened not unto the people; for the cause was from the Lord.” Then Israel answered, “What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David.” They stoned Adoram, made Jeroboam king over all Israel, “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only.”

“So Israel rebelled against the house of David unto this day.” That is where the enmity begins that you keep seeing as Jew and Gentile in the New Testament.

precepts.text: Shemaiah the man of God tells Rehoboam and Judah not to fight their brethren the children of Israel, for the division was from the Most High.
precepts.point: The division began when Rehoboam refused the people and Jeroboam led the ten tribes away, so the southern kingdom (Judah, Benjamin, Levi) and the northern kingdom went their separate ways, and the Levites and a remnant that set their hearts to seek the Most High left the north and came to Judah. This is the same enmity you keep seeing as Jew and Gentile in the New Testament.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
Rehoboam gathered “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin, an hundred and fourscore thousand chosen men” to fight against the house of Israel and bring the kingdom back. But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: “Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me.”

The division was from the Most High. The southern kingdom, Judah and Benjamin, and the northern kingdom went their separate ways, and they were still brethren, “your brethren the children of Israel.” The one of “another nation” in Peter's mouth is that brother, the northern kingdom.

precepts.text: The Levites left their suburbs and, with a remnant out of all the tribes of Israel who set their hearts to seek the Most High, came to Judah and Jerusalem.
precepts.point: The division began when Rehoboam refused the people and Jeroboam led the ten tribes away, so the southern kingdom (Judah, Benjamin, Levi) and the northern kingdom went their separate ways, and the Levites and a remnant that set their hearts to seek the Most High left the north and came to Judah. This is the same enmity you keep seeing as Jew and Gentile in the New Testament.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:

So the southern kingdom was Judah, Benjamin and Levi. And not only the Levites: “after them out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem.” A remnant that set their hearts to seek the Most High left the north and came to Judah.

Jeroboam “ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made.” The north went one way and Judah another, and that is the line Peter speaks of when he says a Jew may not keep company with one of another nation.

precepts.text: Jeroboam sets golden calves in Bethel and Dan, saying, "Behold thy gods, O Israel," and devises a feast in the eighth month out of his own heart.
precepts.point: Jeroboam sealed the split with idolatry, making two golden calves in Bethel and Dan, ordaining a feast of his own in the eighth month, and setting up priests of the lowest people, so the northern kingdom sank deeper and deeper into idol worship. He “made priests of the lowest of the people, which were not of the sons of Levi. And Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, like unto the feast that is in Judah.” A feast of his own, out of his own heart.

From there the northern kingdom sank deeper and deeper into idol worship. That idolatry is why Judah would not keep company with them.

Dan is missing. Dan fell into the idolatry of the golden calf and was absorbed, and so Dan is left out of the sealed tribes. That is how deep the northern kingdom's idolatry went.

precepts.text: Elisha says that but for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah he would not look toward the king of Israel nor see him.
precepts.point: The hatred carried straight through the history. Elisha would not even look toward the king of Israel and dealt only with Jehoshaphat of Judah, and later Pekah of Israel conspired with Rezin of Syria against Judah, which began the exile of the north by the Assyrian kings.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:

The prophet would not even look toward the king of Israel. He dealt only with Jehoshaphat of Judah. That is the same wall Peter speaks of: a Jew did not keep company with the northern kingdom.

“Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to war: and they besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.” The northern kingdom conspired with Syria against Judah, their own brethren.

Ahaz sent to the king of Assyria, “I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me.” He took the silver and gold of the house of the Lord and sent it as a present, and the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, took it, “and slew Rezin.”

That conspiracy of Israel with Syria against Judah is what began the exile of the north by the Assyrian kings.

“For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son.”

Samaria is the parcel of ground Jacob gave to Joseph, Ephraim's land. The woman at the well was dwelling on the inheritance of Joseph's house.

Joseph's two sons are Manasseh and Ephraim, and Ephraim became the head over Samaria. So the parcel of ground Jacob gave to Joseph is Ephraim's land, and a woman of Samaria is of the northern kingdom.

precepts.text: The stick of Judah and the stick of Joseph and Ephraim are joined into one, made one nation, no more two kingdoms, cleansed from their idols.
precepts.point: The restoration is two sticks made one nation. Ephraim, once "not a people," is called back and named the sons of the living God, having obtained mercy that they had not obtained, so the Gentiles being brought in are the outcasts of Israel that Christ came to be a light to.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
The restoration is two sticks made one nation. “Take thee one stick, and write upon it, For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions: then take another stick, and write upon it, For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions: And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand.”

“Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land: And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.”

And Ephraim, joined to idols, is cleansed: “Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols”, “but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them.” That is what God showed Peter: not to call any man common or unclean whom he has cleansed.

precepts.text: In the place where it was said "ye are not my people," there they shall be called the sons of the living God.
precepts.point: The restoration is two sticks made one nation. Ephraim, once "not a people," is called back and named the sons of the living God, having obtained mercy that they had not obtained, so the Gentiles being brought in are the outcasts of Israel that Christ came to be a light to.

Ephraim, once Lo-ammi, “not a people”, is called back and named the sons of the living God. The same house of Israel that was broken and taken away is restored in the very place where it was called not my people.

precepts.text: He will say to them which were not his people, "Thou art my people," and they shall say, "Thou art my God."
precepts.point: The restoration is two sticks made one nation. Ephraim, once "not a people," is called back and named the sons of the living God, having obtained mercy that they had not obtained, so the Gentiles being brought in are the outcasts of Israel that Christ came to be a light to.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

“I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.”

The house of Israel was told “I will no more have mercy”, and here the Most High has mercy on her that had not obtained mercy. Ephraim, who was not his people, is called his people again. That is who God showed Peter not to call common or unclean.
